schools.summary: Ellicott identifies Ahasuerus as Xerxes (485-464 BC), his reign running through Thermopylae and Salamis; Keil summarizes the book's argument. Both set the 127 provinces beside Daniel's 120 satraps.
Clarke, following Prideaux, makes him Artaxerxes Longimanus (third year, c. 462 BC); Wesley makes him Darius Hystaspis, whose wife Atossa recalls Hadassah.
Gill rules out Astyages (Dan. 9:1) and Cambyses (Ezra 4:6) and inclines, with the Midrash, to the Artaxerxes of Ezra and Nehemiah.
Henry, following Lightfoot, takes him for the Artaxerxes who hindered the temple (Ezra 4:6-7); the vast dominion is power for mischief in a bad hand, for good in a good one.

debates.question: Which Persian king is the Ahasuerus of Esther?

sides.position: Xerxes
Artaxerxes Longimanus
Darius Hystaspis
the Artaxerxes of Ezra 4 who hindered the temple

schools.summary: Keil denies that 'sat on the throne' implies peace after wars — it means enthroned with royal authority, as the Persian kings even watched their battles seated; Ellicott fixes Shushan as Susa, the kings' abode.
Clarke and Wesley read a king settled in peaceable possession after subduing his enemies; Clarke renders habbirah 'the city,' and both note Susa the winter capital, Ecbatana the summer.
Gill: fixed and established on the throne, having subdued Egypt in the second year, in great peace and tranquillity.

debates.question: Does 'sat on the throne' mean settled peace after his wars, or simply enthroned royal authority?

sides.position: settled, peaceable possession after subduing his enemies
holders: Clericus and Rambach (as reported by Keil)

sides.position: enthroned with royal authority, implying no lull in war

schools.summary: Ellicott dates the third year to 483 BC and the feast to the war-council for invading Greece; Keil, with Bertheau, reads the circumstantial clause as fixing attention on the assembled forces; both note partemim, the Persian 'first.'
Gill leaves the occasion uncertain — a birthday or an accession-anniversary feast such as Herodotus ascribes to the Persian kings.

debates.question: What was the occasion of the third-year feast?

sides.position: uncertain — the king's birthday or the anniversary of his accession
a council at Susa to plan the invasion of Greece, joined to rejoicing over the Egyptian war

schools.summary: Ellicott calls a six-month banquet incredible, reading the 180 days as the time troops were gathered; Keil argues the text does not call it a feast at all, the seven-day banquet of v.5 being the feast proper.
Wesley takes it as one continuous festival, every day a feast; Clarke expounds Persian luxury as proverbial (Horace's 'Persicos odi, puer, apparatus').
Gill sees the richest of Persian kings displaying his wealth to animate his nobles for the Grecian expedition, fulfilling Daniel 11:2.

debates.question: What were the hundred and eighty days?

sides.position: a literal half-year of continuous feasting
not a feast but a period of displaying wealth and mustering the invasion of Greece

schools.summary: Keil carries the narrative into the seven days in the garden court; Ellicott sets the feast for 'all the people' beside Cyrus feasting all the Persians (Herodotus).
Clarke marks the descent from a feast for nobles to one for the people at large, held in the garden court because no hall could hold them.
Gill: when the 180 days of the nobles' feast were ended, the king feasted the whole city, great and small.
Henry weighs it as vain glory — better a dinner of herbs with quietness (Prov. 15:17) than this banquet of wine; the history falls between Ezra 6 and 7.

themes: all the people, great and small

schools.summary: Ellicott corrects the colours to things: 'white cotton and blue,' and the pavement-words to named stones (malachite, white marble, pearl, black); white and blue the royal colours of Persia.
Clarke describes the canopy on cords, the coloured pavement as the origin of Mosaic work, and the golden couches; Wesley explains the 'beds' as reclining couches.
Gill reads white, green (carpas), and blue linen hangings, the enlarged letter marking their whiteness.

debates.question: Are carpas and the pavement-words colours or things?

sides.position: colours — green linen, and marbles of red, blue, white, and black
white cotton, and the pavement named precious stones, not colours

themes: the hangings of the garden court

schools.summary: Keil hears an exclamatory Hebrew of profusion; Ellicott reads 'according to the hand of a king' as royal open-handedness, the wine perhaps that of Helbon (Ezek. 27:18).
Gill: the diverse golden vessels proclaim royal wealth, and — against the Targum — these are not the temple vessels, long since restored to Zerubbabel (Ezra 1).
Clarke: the guests were served from different services of plate.
Clarke heaps up the Greek and Roman customs of forced drinking (the arbiter bibendi, Herbert's verses) that the king's law overturns; Wesley makes the heathen restraint a rebuke to Christian tables.
Ellicott reads 'law' as a special ordinance for the occasion, notable since the Persians were once temperate; Keil: the officers served each man at his pleasure.
Gill: none compelled to drink beyond his choice, against the degenerate Persian excess Xenophon describes.
Henry praises the absence of forced healths and warns from Habakkuk 2:15-16 against sending the sin round.

debates.question: Was the drinking-rule a standing law or a special ordinance for the feast?

sides.position: a law (some lately made) against compelling drink
an ordinance issued specially for this occasion

schools.summary: Ellicott takes up Vashti's history — a supreme wife like Atossa — and the Greek Amestris, doubting Rawlinson's and Wordsworth's identifications and refusing to equate Esther with Amestris.
Clarke and Wesley explain the separate women's feast by Persian custom, the sexes never feasting together; Clarke reads the name as 'beautiful.'
Gill: the queen feasts apart by custom; her identity is disputed (Atossa, or Evilmerodach's daughter), the name akin to Vesta, 'vehement fire.'
Henry: while the king showed his majesty, Vashti and her ladies showed their modesty, the true majesty of the sex.

sides.position: Atossa, daughter of Cyrus
the daughter of Evilmerodach
Amestris, queen of Xerxes, under another name
not to be identified with Amestris

schools.summary: Henry: a damp to all the mirth — the king's drunken folly dishonoured him as husband (Gen. 20:16) and diminished him as king; when the wine is in, the wit is out.
Keil: the wine had made him merry; Ellicott renders 'eunuchs' and finds in the seven named men a writer of personal knowledge.
Clarke: the names are Persian disguised through Hebrew, Mehuman meaning a stranger or guest.
Gill: the seventh and last day was, by Jarchi and the Targum, the sabbath.

themes: the seventh day, merry with wine

schools.summary: Ellicott: a sober king would never have asked it, and Vashti naturally refuses; the crown royal a jewelled cap with the blue-and-white diadem (Trench).
Clarke reports the Targum's tradition that she was to be brought naked, and ties her name 'beautiful' to 'fair to look on.'
Gill softens the order to a summons, not force — the king's pleasure that she come at once.

debates.question: Was the command an innocent summons or an indecent demand?

sides.position: a bare summons, the king's pleasure that she come
an indecent demand, plainly the fruit of drink

schools.summary: Clarke praises Vashti as a noble woman refusing to expose herself to drunken revellers; Wesley: the law of Persia favoured her refusal.
Gill defends her — she judged the king drunk, and Persian law barred wives from public view, so the summons treated her as a harlot.
Keil: she would not stake her dignity as queen and wife before his inebriated guests.
Henry alone hesitates — the thing was not sinful, and obedience might have been her honour, unless she refused haughtily; the deeper folly was the king's, ruling 127 provinces but not his own spirit.

debates.question: How is Vashti's refusal to be judged?

sides.position: modest courage, wholly praiseworthy
not clearly wise — obedience might have been more honourable, unless she refused haughtily

themes: no rule over his own spirit

schools.summary: The school divides: Keil reads the wise men as astrologers and magi (cf. Dan. 2:27; Isa. 47:13); Ellicott as men skilled in legal precedent; both note the king's settled habit of consulting law and judgment.
Clarke guesses them the lawyers; Wesley the men who knew the histories of former times.
Gill offers both — astrologers (Aben Ezra) or men learned in history.

debates.question: Who were 'the wise men which knew the times'?

sides.position: astrologers and magi, reading the heavens
jurists skilled in law and precedent
historians who knew former times

themes: the wise men who knew the times
an absolute king bound to counsel

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the seven as heads of Persia's leading families, the 'seven counsellors' of Ezra 7:14, and ventures Marsena=Mardonius, Admatha=Artabanus; Keil notes Memucan, named last, will be spokesman.
Clarke: the privy counsellors admitted to the royal presence; Wesley: seeing the king's face meant rare access to a seldom-seen king.
Gill: 'the next unto him' is the man nearest the king, first in dignity and authority.
Henry: though the queen was guilty the law must have its course, and the angry king would do only what was according to law; the greater the power, the greater the need of counsel (Prov. 11:14).
Keil: the incensed king inquires what is to be done to Vashti according to law, not what his anger dictates.
Gill: the king desired to know what law was provided for such a case.

themes: what to do according to law
a private slight made a public cause

schools.summary: The school divides on Memucan: Keil reports his verdict straight — Vashti wronged all the princes and people; Ellicott reads him a courtier echoing the king's anger ('dealt unfairly').
Clarke calls the reasoning inconsequent and false — a single act made a sweeping precedent, the rest too drunk or too eager for mastery to object.
Gill: Memucan, least and youngest, spoke first, as puisne judges give their opinion before the elder.
Henry grants a possibly honest motive — Josephus says the king loved Vashti, so Memucan may have had sincere regard for justice and the public good.

debates.question: Was Memucan's counsel sound or a flatterer's overreach?

sides.position: false and inconsequent, flattery echoing the king's anger
possibly a sincere regard for justice and the public good

schools.summary: Henry: a public example would embolden all wives; the contentions of a wife a continual dropping (Prov. 19:13; 27:15), against the reverence of Eph. 5:33 and the subjection of 1 Pet. 3:1 — yet the fear is also exaggerated.
Gill: the deed will spread through the dominions and become the common talk of every wife.
Keil: the counsellor builds his case for a decree on the certainty that the refusal cannot stay hidden.

themes: the court as pattern to the realm
a fear at once shrewd and comic

schools.summary: Ellicott mends the tense so the threat lands 'this day,' and resolves 'contempt and wrath' into the wives' defiance and the husbands' anger.
Clarke recovers the 'princesses' beneath 'ladies'; Wesley reads contempt in the wives, wrath in the husbands, and strife in families.
Gill: from this day the princesses will give their husbands the like refusal.
Henry: contempt, wrath, and strife breed confusion and every evil work (James 3:16); the great must beware the copies they set.

themes: the princesses of Persia and Media

schools.summary: Ellicott reads 'that it pass not away' — the written order immutable, as in Daniel's case (Dan. 6:8) and Esther 8:8; Keil renders the proposal 'a word of the kingdom.'
Clarke: the decree inserted among the unchangeable laws of the Medes and Persians.
Gill: not a mere proclamation but a law enacted by royal authority.
Henry: Vashti to come no more before the king, her estate given to another, and this never to be reversed.

themes: laws of the Medes and Persians
a rigidity that will trap the king

schools.summary: Keil: the decree published through the empire in every province's script and speech (cf. Esther 8:9), that all wives render honour.
Henry: wives of great and small to honour their husbands, every man ruling his house — states have an interest in good order in families.
Gill: fit that the decree be published everywhere, since the queen's deed would travel as far.

themes: reverence beyond the reach of statute

schools.summary: Henry: whether passion or policy was served, God's providence made way for Esther to the crown and defeated Haman before his plot was formed — the Lord reigns and overrules the folly of men.
Keil: the king carried the counsel into execution, sending letters to teach every husband to rule his house.
Gill: the king and the six other princes unanimously approved the proposal.

Ellicott notes the Persian postal system and the 'compel' word of Matt. 5:41, and reads the last clause literally — the husband to keep his own tongue dominant, the AV doing violence to the Hebrew; Keil takes it of publishing in each people's speech (cf. Esther 8:9).
Gill: letters to all 127 provinces, sealed with the king's own seal.
Clarke: the decree established nothing new, a parade of legislation only to strip Vashti of her crown.

debates.question: What does the decree's last clause mean?

sides.position: the edict published to each people in its own language
the husband to keep his own language dominant at home — the AV mistranslating

outliers.note: Dismisses the whole enactment as establishing nothing that God's law and common sense had not taught from the foundation of the world — a mere pretext to deprive Vashti of her crown.

themes: each people in its own tongue
